subject: chemistry
title: Atoms, elements, compounds and formulae
key_idea: All substances are made of **atoms**. An **element** contains only one type of atom. A **compound** contains two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions. Symbols and formulae are the shorthand for them.

blocks.text: Everything is built from atoms. This section covers how atoms make up elements and compounds.

items.meaning: The smallest part of an element that can exist.
A substance made of only one type of atom. There are about 100 different elements.
A substance of two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.
A change that forms one or more new substances, often with a detectable energy change.

items: Elements are shown in the periodic table.
Compounds are formed from elements by chemical reactions.
Compounds can only be separated back into elements by chemical reactions.
A compound has a fixed ratio of atoms. Water is always two hydrogen atoms for every one oxygen atom.

diagram.alt: Sort each substance into element or compound.

items: An element has one type of atom. A compound has two or more types, chemically combined.
Compounds are made by chemical reactions and can only be split by chemical reactions.
The atoms in a compound are in a fixed ratio.

blocks.text: Each element has a chemical symbol of one or two letters. The first letter is always a capital and the second is always lower case.
The Group 1 and Group 7 elements are on the periodic table you are given in the exam, so use it to check symbols.

items: A formula uses the symbols of the elements in the compound.
A small number after a symbol, written lower, says how many atoms of that element. No number means one atom.
A number after a bracket multiplies everything inside the bracket.
Some elements exist as molecules of two atoms: H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂.

blocks.text: Naming a compound from its formula

items: A name ending **-ide** usually means the compound has just those two elements: sodium chloride, NaCl.
A name ending **-ate** means the compound also has oxygen: copper sulfate, CuSO₄.
Name the metal first, then the non-metal.
A symbol has a capital letter first, then a lower-case letter if there is a second.
In a formula, the small number says how many atoms. No number means one.
A number after a bracket multiplies every atom inside it.

blocks.text: Chemical reactions are written as word equations or as equations using symbols and formulae.

blocks.label: A symbol equation for the same reaction
where: The big numbers in front balance the number of atoms on each side.
Never change the small numbers inside a formula.

items.text: Write the names of the reactants and products.
Replace each name with its correct formula.
Put numbers in front of formulae until each element has the same number of atoms on both sides.

items: (s) means solid and (l) means liquid.
(g) means gas. H₂O(g) is water vapour, also called steam.
(aq) means aqueous: dissolved in water.

blocks.text: (AQA: Higher tier) You also write half equations and ionic equations. Those are covered in later topics.

items: A word equation uses names. A symbol equation uses formulae.
Balance an equation with big numbers in front of formulae, never by changing a formula.

checks.q: Describe the difference between an element and a compound.
checks.a: An element contains only one type of atom. A compound contains two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.

checks.q: How many atoms of each element are there in one unit of Ca(NO₃)₂?
Name the elements with the symbols Na, Mg and Cl.

worked_example.question:
This question is about gases. Match each substance to the description of the substance.

Substances: air, carbon dioxide, oxygen.

Descriptions: compound, element, hydrocarbon, metal, mixture.
worked_example.tip: One mark for each correct match. Only one description can be chosen for each substance.

worked_example.question:
Fertilisers contain compounds of different elements.
Three of these elements have the symbols K, N and P.
Use the periodic table to state the names of these three elements.
worked_example.tip: All three correct scores 2 marks. One or two correct scores 1 mark.

worked_example.question:
A student investigates the reaction between acids and metals.

The table shows the names and formulae of the acids and metals the student investigates.

Zinc: Zn
Magnesium: ______
Nitric acid: HNO₃
Hydrochloric acid: ______

Complete the table.
worked_example.tip: One mark for each correct formula.

worked_example.question:
Sulfur is a Group VI element.
An acid containing sulfur reacts with sodium hydroxide, NaOH, to form a salt and water. The salt has the formula Na₂SO₃.
Deduce the formula of this acid.
worked_example.tip: The two sodium ions in the salt replaced two hydrogen ions in the acid.

items: Deduce a formula from a diagram or model: count the atoms of each element in one unit, then write the symbols with those numbers.
A **mixture** contains two or more substances that are not chemically combined. Its parts keep their own properties and can be in any proportions.
A compound has different properties from the elements in it. A mixture keeps the properties of its parts.
Know the formulae of the compounds named in the course, for example HCl, H₂SO₄, NaOH, NH₃, CaCO₃, Na₂CO₃, Zn(NO₃)₂ and (NH₄)₂SO₄.
A Roman numeral in a name gives the charge on the metal ion. Iron(III) oxide is Fe₂O₃ and manganese(II) oxide is MnO.

worked_example.question:
This question is about elements, mixtures and compounds.
Explain why silicon dioxide is a compound.
answer_points: It contains two different types of atom (silicon and oxygen)
worked_example.tip: One mark for two different elements and one for them being chemically joined.

items.meaning: Two or more atoms joined together by chemical bonds, such as H₂, O₂ or H₂O.
Two or more substances that are not chemically combined. Each keeps its own properties.

items: To classify a substance, ask how many types of atom it has and whether they are chemically joined.
One type of atom only: an element.
Different atoms chemically joined in a fixed ratio: a compound.
Different substances not chemically joined: a mixture.
